thread.title: Morning Movers: Juno Soars on Celgene Takeout; GE Slumps on Merrill Cut

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Morning Movers: Juno Soars on Celgene Takeout; GE Slumps on Merrill Cut
text:
No government, no problem? Not quite. Stocks look set to for a lower this morning as the standoff in the Senate over the budget continues into its third day. S&P 500 futures have dipped 0.1%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have fallen 49 points, or 0.2%. Nasdaq Composite futures are little changed. And with little in the way of economic data—just a stronger-than-expected Chicago Fed National Activity Index—or earnings—see below—to keep us warm, it will take dip buying to get this market moving higher.
Illustration: Getty Images Contrast that with Europe, where Germany's Social Democrats agreed to negotiate with Angela Merkel on a new government, something that could pave the way for her to serve a fourth term as that country's leader. Germany's DAX has advanced 0.2% to 13,457.65. The Euro Stoxx 50 has gained 0.4% to 3,662.61.
We'll also be keeping an eye on the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield, which is trying to break higher . As of this writing, it's trading at around 2.65% , above important resistance levels, but not really breaking out. With stocks at a standstill, expect yields to get much of the attention.
— Ben Levisohn
Morning Movers
Juno Therapeutics (JUNO) has soared up 27% to $86.26 after it agreed to be bought by Celgene (CELG), for $87 a share in cash, or $9 billion. The news isn't a total surprise, as rumors of a deal circulated last week. Celgene has fallen 2% to $100.60 on the news, but at least one analyst likes the deal. "We believe the transaction (expected to close 1Q18) is likely to be viewed favorably by investors as it allow Celgene to stay at the forefront of cellular therapy, helps diversify the business away from the myeloma franchise, and was conducted at a fair price," SunTrust Robinson Humphrey analyst Yatin Suneja wrote in a note this morning.
Halliburton (HAL) has gained 3.2% to $54.70 after it reported better-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings. The oilfield services giant said it earned 53 cents a share, on revenue that rose 47.7% year over year to $5.94 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of 46 cents a share, on revenue of $5.63 billion.
General Electric (GE) has dropped 1.4% to $16.03 after Bank of America Merrill Lynch downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy. The move comes after yet another hard week for GE last week, when analysts worried it may have to raise equity capital after it took a $15 billion charge to bolster capital reserves at its insurance unit.
Eli Lilly (LLY) has slumped 2.2% to $83.60 after Credit Suisse downgraded the stock to Underperform from Neutral. Last week, Goldman Sachs a lso cut their rating on Eli Lilly to Neutral from Buy, citing concerns about the stock's valuation.
Wynn Resorts (WYNN) has climbed 4.1% to $186.93 after reporting Street beating earnings. The casino operator reported a profit of $1.490 a share , beating forecasts for $1.38. Sales came in at $1.69 billion, topping estimates for $1.57 billion. — Teresa Rivas
An Eye on...Utilities
The power has gone out for utilities stocks.
As Barron's Lawrence S. Strauss noted this weekend, "more than most sectors, utility stocks have felt the sting of rising interest rates ." And the numbers bear hi out: The Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLU) has slumped 5.1% so far this year, losing nearly as much as the S&P 500 has gained.
But pain often leads to opportunity. MKM technical analyst Jonathan Krinsky notes that as interest rates have risen, utilities have dropped--so much so that its 14-week relative strength indicator has dropped to its lowest level since 2009, a sign that the group is quite oversold. "We think this creates the set-up for a tactical bounce in the group, even if it proves to be short-lived," Krinsky says.
Is the power about to go back on? — B.L
The View From Silicon Valley
Facebook Let's Users Rate the News
Front and center this morning is Facebook (FB), which appears to be serious about cleaning up its tattered image. The question is: Will investors buy in?
Starting today, the social networking giant will let its 2 billion members rank the credibility and trustworthiness of news organizations , based on regular surveys.
Illustration: Bloomberg News In a Friday post, Facebook Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg wrote it is the responsibility of social media companies to help prevent the spread of fake news and misinformation. “We decided that having the community determine which sources are broadly trusted would be most objective,” he said.
The sweeping change is the latest sign of Facebook’s self-regulation amid widespread criticism that it, Google ( GOOGL ) and Twitter ( TWTR ) were fonts of misinformation during the 2016 presidential election and require some form of governmental oversight. A week earlier, Facebook vowed to show fewer posts from publishers and brands to encourage more interactions between friends and family. Investors initially reacted by sending Facebook shares down sharply.
Will history repeat today? If nothing else, Facebook’s news-credibility initiative could have unintended consequences on what news will be consumed, favoring more familiar brands at the expense of lesser-known media operations. — Jon Swartz
Tech M&A on the Way?
Could 2018 be the year of mergers and acquisitions in tech? Ajeet Singh thinks so.
The CEO of business-data analytics company ThoughtSpot, who co-founded Nutanix (NTNX), the largest tech IPO of 2016, predicts tax cut windfalls will spur a boatload of deals.
Flush with billions of dollars from a lower corporate tax rate and changes to repatriation, companies like Apple (AAPL), Google and Microsoft (MSFT) could “go on massive buying sprees,” he says.
Singh expects activity around companies in artificial intelligence, mixed reality and big data as tech’s bigger players look for a competitive edge in innovation.
For another view on tech M&A , read Tiernan Ray's Tech Trader column. — J.S.
